title: Black lung rates in Appalachia are high as the 1970s, with thousands of miners sick

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

Respiratory therapist Marcy Freeman doesn't need a research study to confirm for her a return to the dark days of coal mining. She finds evidence in a stack of more than 150 funeral programs, all for former patients at her pulmonary rehabilitation clinic in Norton, Virginia.

"Each one of these represents a life that's gone because of black lung," Freeman explained as she flipped through the programs, recognizing names and images.

Related Story: NPR

"These are husbands. These are brothers. … These men were just hardworking men, and the only thing they did was go to work and provide for their families. And it cost them everything. … This is the aftermath of black lung."

This aftermath is more dire than even black lung clinicians and researchers expected, according to new data published Wednesday in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 

The data appears in a peer-reviewed research letter from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), a federal research agency.

Public Health Watch, Kentucky Public Radio and NPR obtained a draft of the NIOSH research letter before publication.

NIOSH researchers found that working veteran underground coal miners in central Appalachia are suffering from the incurable and fatal lung disease at the highest rates in nearly 50 years.

Miners working in Kentucky, Virginia and West Virginia who've had at least 25 years underground have the worst rate of coal workers' pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease. One in three — 32.5% — tested positive in X-rays conducted by NIOSH during the last five years.

The last time the rate of disease was that high for miners with the same work history was 1978. In 2018, when NIOSH last reported rates of the disease, the rate was 20.6%.

The new research shows that even miners with as few as 15 years underground have higher rates of black lung — rates not seen in nearly 40 years.

Related Story: NPR

"I'm disgusted," said Scott Laney, a NIOSH research epidemiologist who is the lead author of the research letter.

"This is not going to get better because of all the disease that's already in the pipeline. These guys are being treated like disposable widgets, not human beings. … We're watching them die right before our eyes."

More than 1,700 coal miners died from black lung from 2020 through 2023, according to an earlier NIOSH study.

Kentucky Public Radio and its reporting partners provided the federal Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) a summary of the NIOSH findings, but the agency declined to comment or respond to questions before seeing the published report.

"Coal miners are no better off"

The new findings "should stagger and shock anyone who has compassion for … hardworking people," said Celeste Monforton, a former federal mine-safety regulator and a workplace-safety academic and advocate.

"This is the consequence of their work and the consequence of us wanting cheap electricity," Monforton added. "We're back where we were [nearly 50 years ago]. … Coal miners are no better off than they were [then]."

Related Story: NPR

The newly published findings do not include the number of miners tested or diagnosed in the five-year period used to determine the rate of disease. But in response to questions from Public Health Watch and Kentucky Public Radio, NIOSH said it screened 280 working veteran underground miners in central Appalachia in the past five years, with 91 testing positive for black lung. The agency used that sample to estimate a rate for all similar miners in the region, an approach used since 1974.

"The overall process" that NIOSH researchers applied here "is valid in my opinion," said Akshay Sood, a clinical and research pulmonologist specializing in occupational lung diseases, including black lung, at the University of New Mexico School of Medicine. Sood reviewed a draft of the NIOSH research letter at the request of NPR, Kentucky Public Radio and Public Health Watch.

The NIOSH study "reinforces prior observations that disease prevalence continues to increase despite modern dust-control regulations," Sood concluded.

The NIOSH researchers also wrote that "multiple external indicators … demonstrate patterns consistent" with their findings, including thousands of new cases of disease diagnosed by black lung clinics in the last decade.

The new estimated rate for the veteran central Appalachian underground miners is more than a fourfold increase since the prevalence of the disease hit a low point: just 7%, in 1999. That was 30 years after Congress imposed strict limits on exposure to the coal mine dust that causes black lung.

Since then, the dramatic plunge has reversed, especially in Appalachia, where thousands of miners are suffering from early, advanced and fatal stages of disease, according to data gathered from clinics testing and treating miners. Unlike NIOSH, which focuses on working miners, the clinics tend to see retired and laid-off miners who seek lung exams while trying to obtain state or federal black lung benefits.

The clinics have been inundated with miners in the wake of coal mine closures. More than 15,000 workers across the U.S. lost coal mine jobs in the last decade, according to employment data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

"It's awful," said Brandon Crum, a radiologist in Coal Run Village, Kentucky, who specializes in detecting signs of black lung in X-rays. In 2016, Crum first documented an alarming spike in severe black lung — as well as rapid progression of the disease — among younger and younger coal miners. NIOSH researchers and an NPR investigation confirmed his findings.

The new NIOSH research indicates to Crum that the trend continues.

"It's just another thing that proves what we've been saying for the last 10 years," he said. "And this may be even worse than what we thought it was going to be."

The National Mining Association (NMA), the leading industry trade group, was also provided a summary of the NIOSH findings. NMA noted that the rates of disease reported by NIOSH in miners tested in the last five years — along with the new cases diagnosed at clinics — do not stem from current silica dust exposures in coal mines because it can take years for disease to develop and for disease to be diagnosed.

"This means that the incidences discussed in these studies cover miners whose initial exposure dates back years and, in many cases, decades," Ashley Burke, a spokeswoman for NMA, wrote in an emailed statement. "These incidences do not reflect the conditions, practices, protections or regulations that are in place today."

Still, miner advocates are concerned that high rates of disease will continue because of a major change in coal mining that's causing dangerous dust exposure.

Cutting through rocks

In recent decades, the biggest coal seams in Appalachia were mined out. Mining companies turned to the thinner seams that remained, digging through mountains to reach and then mine them. That requires cutting lots of rock, and in Appalachia, that rock typically contains quartz, which is rich in silica. The result is clouds of both coal dust and highly toxic silica dust.

"Excessive inhalation of coal mine dust is the sole cause of [black lung] in coal miners," the new NIOSH research letter says. "Substantial evidence shows that exposure to the respirable crystalline silica component of coal mine dust plays an important role in contemporary disease patterns."

Laney, the NIOSH epidemiologist, said the link between silica dust and black lung disease is strong, based on exposure data and radiographic data, which shows abnormalities "suggestive of silica exposure." And he said researchers have inspected lungs removed in autopsies and after transplantation and "we can see the silica in these lungs."

Silica dust is 20 times more toxic than coal dust alone and contains fine particles that are easily inhaled. Silica particles cause lungs to fight back with fibrotic tissue that builds and builds, severely inhibiting the ability to breathe.

Coal miners who've worked underground in the last 25 years have witnessed the changes that led to more silica dust exposure.

"The thickness of the coal is not there," explained Tim Balthis, a former miner and mine foreman in Kentucky and Virginia. It's not like the days when the "grandpas" mined the big coal seams, he said. "So you're having to take more rock, which in turn creates silica dust."

Balthis spoke at New Beginnings Pulmonary Rehab, one of four black lung clinics owned and operated by Freeman, the respiratory therapist. The clinics help miners ease symptoms of the incurable disease.

At 57, Balthis has what is called complicated black lung, the advanced and fatal stage. He tried to describe for non-miners what it's like working around silica dust in an underground coal mine.

"It's like opening your front door and letting the sunshine [in]" with dust particles floating in the light. "And then multiply that by 10 billion times. … It's like a fog," Balthis recalled.

"Thousands of opportunities for disease"

The National Mining Association cites government data that shows increasing compliance with silica dust exposure limits in the last 10 years, with mining companies nationwide meeting those limits more than 90% of the time. Last year, the compliance rate hit 97%.

But a high rate of compliance doesn't mean miners are fully protected. The small percentage of overexposures has translated to thousands of instances in which miners are put at risk.

Kentucky Public Radio and Public Health Watch analyzed MSHA silica dust sampling data and found that coal miners were exposed to excessive levels of silica dust more than 5,000 times since 2014. Silica particles are so toxic, so easily inhaled, and so easily embedded in lungs, that "thousands of exposures equate to thousands of opportunities for disease," said former regulator Monforton.

In fact, an NPR and FRONTLINE investigation in 2018 documented 21,000 instances of overexposure to silica dust in a review of 30 years of federal data. The news organizations also documented a growing number of retired and laid-off miners stricken with complicated black lung, a count that now exceeds 4,000 since 2010.

"A love affair with the black rock"

NIOSH first recommended tougher limits on silica dust exposure in coal mines in 1974. But for 50 years, both Democratic and Republican administrations failed to act. That finally changed in 2024, when the Biden administration succeeded in establishing a new silica dust regulation for mining. It made the exposure limit twice as restrictive. It also provided, for the first time, a direct regulatory response to overexposure, including imposition of even tougher exposure restrictions, and possible fines, for noncompliance.

But the mining industry sued, agreeing with the tougher exposure limit but not the enforcement mechanism.

Federal courts responded to the industry lawsuits, which also cite other issues, with an indefinite delay in enforcement of the tougher silica exposure limits. The Trump administration did not oppose the delay, announcing it too would put enforcement on hold.

Related Story: NPR

And the Trump administration is trying to boost coal mining. In early June, Trump announced close to $700 million in federal spending to sustain coal-burning power plants and to support exports of coal.

"Coal's a great business," Trump said at the time. "In terms of power, there's nothing like it."

Monforton said the administration seems to have "a love affair with the black rock, and not a love affair or compassion or concern for coal miners."

Mining companies are required to control dust exposure with robust ventilation underground. Mining machines must also have water sprays that tamp down dust. But sometimes, they don't work well enough to keep the dust down.

The coal mining industry wants to be able to require the use of dust masks, so that miners could still work when other control measures fail.

"When other controls do not adequately reduce exposure levels, those extensive controls will be supplemented with respirators, which is no different than any other profession that requires the use of masks to ensure air quality safety," the NMA's Burke said.

But federal law treats underground coal mining differently from other industries. The Mine Safety and Health Act requires coal mining companies to prevent "unsafe and unhealthful conditions" and to make sure miners can work their entire careers in working conditions "sufficiently free of respirable dust" so they don't fall victim to black lung.

Dust masks and respirators have also been problematic. Many miners interviewed by NPR complained that masks impair communication in a dangerous and noisy environment, become clogged with dust, are too hot to work in, and fail to screen out finer particles. Lawsuits against dust-mask companies have resulted in multimillion-dollar verdicts and settlements.

Even more modern devices have issues, including helmets that push fresh air down across the face and behind a clear shield. MSHA noted in its 2024 silica dust regulation that the helmets "are not a permanent solution" because they make it difficult to communicate effectively, and may limit peripheral vision and situational awareness, which can make work hazardous.

Dr. Drew Harris, a University of Virginia pulmonologist, who is also medical director at the Stone Mountain black lung clinics in Virginia, is direct about delayed protections for coal miners.

"We need to act and we need the will to act," Harris asserted. "We need to enforce the protections that we know will work to make this disease go away."

"Folks that don't have a voice" 

Harris' black lung clinics in southwestern Virginia, Stone Mountain Health Services, see more miners and diagnose more cases of disease than any clinic in the country. Miners from coal counties across Appalachia flock to Stone Mountain because it provides testing, treatment and legal help with black lung benefits claims.

Harris called the new findings from NIOSH "outrageous." But they're not surprising based on what he's been seeing in the clinics. In just the past five years alone, Stone Mountain has diagnosed 2,400 new cases of black lung.

"If you imagine one out of every three school teachers were getting an incurable lung disease because of something they were exposed to at work, the whole country would put their hands up screaming, and stop whatever this exposure was immediately," Harris said. "[But] this is largely impacting rural Appalachian folks that don't have a voice, that don't have a country to unite behind them."

The growing rate of disease has resulted in a steady stream of miners seeking state and federal benefits for living and medical expenses. More than 26,000 miners or their surviving dependents drew $175 million from a federal black lung trust fund in 2024, according to a Labor Department report to Congress.

Mining companies contributed more than $23 billion to the fund, according to NMA, but bankruptcies and underinsurance shift some of the burden to taxpayers. The fund owes more than $6.5 billion to the U.S. Treasury.

Public funds pay for most of a growing number of lung transplants, which cost as much as $2 million each, and are mostly for miners in central Appalachia, according to a NIOSH study. 

The black lung burden for miners like Tim Balthis makes life itself challenging. Even the simplest tasks are difficult as fibrotic tissue builds up in his lungs. Breathing becomes more and more labored. He knows it will only get worse. He's likely to die from it, unless he qualifies for a lung transplant. But even that, for coal miners, comes with a median survival rate of less than seven years.

"It's like a cut in your manhood." Balthis said, noting that he carries and uses an "emergency inhaler" to get more than a few minutes of playing time with his grandchildren or even singing at church.

"I've had several doctors say that I should already be dead… And I tell them this…'God's not done with me yet.' I've been obedient to Him, and now He's giving me back to my grandbabies…He's not finished with me.'"

Transcript

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:

Federal health researchers at the CDC have a new report today about black lung disease among the most experienced coal miners in Appalachia. They are suffering from the incurable disease at the highest rates in nearly half a century. Justin Hicks with the Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom reports.

(SOUNDBITE OF MACHINERY BEEPING)

JUSTIN HICKS, BYLINE: Fifty-seven-year-old Tim Balthis visits New Beginnings Pulmonary Rehab in Norton, Virginia, twice a week. He lives with an advanced stage of black lung disease, and here he does light exercises, like walking on a treadmill at just two miles an hour, to help strengthen his lungs.

TIM BALTHIS: This is a normal walking pace for me. If I'm doing this pace, not talking, but I'm carrying something, that gets you out of air, too.

HICKS: Balthis knows there is no cure, but he hopes regular checkups and exercises will grant him more time to celebrate milestones like family birthdays and graduations.

BALTHIS: God's not done with me yet. I've been obedient to him, and now he's giving me back to see my grandbabies.

HICKS: New Beginnings director Marcy Freeman says more miners are coming through her doors. What scares her is that they're younger, and their lung disease is advancing more rapidly.

MARCY FREEMAN: I've never seen patients like this. I've never seen them this sick, this rapid of progression. It's just amazing to me that these men are able to walk around and live and breathe - that they're alive.

HICKS: Today, researchers at the CDC's National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health published new research. It indicates rates of black lung disease in central Appalachia are as high as they were half a century ago. As many as a third of longtime working underground coal miners may have the disease. Lead researcher Scott Laney says these rates of disease rival the 1970s. That's when Congress passed a law requiring mine inspections and dust control standards. And for two decades, disease rates plummeted. Laney says the recent growth is due to mining operations digging the thinner coal seams left in the region. Separating those small amounts of coal from a mountain requires cutting through lots of rock, which generates toxic silica dust.

SCOTT LANEY: Now we're seeing almost all of these miners with mixed-dust pneumoconiosis, which includes silica and coal dust.

HICKS: The National Mining Association represents coal companies, and they say safety measures to mitigate dusty mines have improved, and sick miners could have been exposed years ago, before new technology was in place. But Laney says there is no question in his mind, but the prevalence of black lung disease is still growing. In the research, he wrote, the data is a bellwether, not the remnant of an ongoing problem.

LANEY: Nobody is doubting this whatsoever - I mean, especially if you live here in Appalachia like we do. You see it at the post office and the grocery store every day.

HICKS: To curb this growing problem, the Federal Mine Safety and Health Administration created stricter limits on the amount of silica dust coal miners can legally be exposed to. But mining companies sued. The Mining Association says they support lower dust limits, but they want allowances for other methods to protect miners, like dust-filtering helmets. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has frozen enforcement indefinitely. That delay really frustrates Drew Harris, a lung doctor in southwest Virginia, who treats patients suffering with black lung disease.

DREW HARRIS: It's outrageous that these are the numbers we see in 2026. We know how to prevent it. There's no mystery here. We need better protections to be enforced.

HICKS: The Mine Safety and Health Administration declined to comment until the research letter was public. But legal briefs show the federal mining agency is holding private meetings around changing the safety rules. So for now, it's still unclear what future silica dust protections may or may not be in store for coal miners.

For NPR News, I'm Justin Hicks in Norton, Virginia.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

Correction

Aug. 6th, 2026

An earlier version of this story mistakenly implied Congress imposed strict limits on exposure to coal mine dust in 1977. In fact, those limits were imposed in 1969. It also incorrectly said the federal black lung trust fund owes $3 billion to the U.S. Treasury; it owes $6.5 billion. And an earlier caption misidentified the person scrutinizing an X-ray image as radiologist Brandon Crum in Coal Run Village, Ky. The person is a clinician at New Beginnings Pulmonary Rehab in Norton, Va.

I've been obedient to Him, and now He's giving me back to my grandbabies…He's not finished with me.'"This story was produced as a collaboration between NPR; Public Health Watch, an independent nonprofit investigative newsroom focused on public, environmental and occupational health; Kentucky Public Radio; the Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom; and the PBS series FRONTLINE. Transcript MICHEL MARTIN, HOST: Federal health researchers at the CDC have a new report today about black lung disease among the most experienced coal miners in Appalachia. They are suffering from the incurable disease at the highest rates in nearly half a century. Justin Hicks with the Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom reports.(SOUNDBITE OF MACHINERY BEEPING)JUSTIN HICKS, BYLINE: Fifty-seven-year-old Tim Balthis visits New Beginnings Pulmonary Rehab in Norton, Virginia, twice a week. He lives with an advanced stage of black lung disease, and here he does light exercises, like walking on a treadmill at just two miles an hour, to help strengthen his lungs.TIM BALTHIS: This is a normal walking pace for me. If I'm doing this pace, not talking, but I'm carrying something, that gets you out of air, too.HICKS: Balthis knows there is no cure, but he hopes regular checkups and exercises will grant him more time to celebrate milestones like family birthdays and graduations.BALTHIS: God's not done with me yet. I've been obedient to him, and now he's giving me back to see my grandbabies.HICKS: New Beginnings director Marcy Freeman says more miners are coming through her doors. What scares her is that they're younger, and their lung disease is advancing more rapidly.MARCY FREEMAN: I've never seen patients like this. I've never seen them this sick, this rapid of progression. It's just amazing to me that these men are able to walk around and live and breathe - that they're alive.HICKS: Today, researchers at the CDC's National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health published new research. It indicates rates of black lung disease in central Appalachia are as high as they were half a century ago. As many as a third of longtime working underground coal miners may have the disease. Lead researcher Scott Laney says these rates of disease rival the 1970s. That's when Congress passed a law requiring mine inspections and dust control standards. And for two decades, disease rates plummeted. Laney says the recent growth is due to mining operations digging the thinner coal seams left in the region. Separating those small amounts of coal from a mountain requires cutting through lots of rock, which generates toxic silica dust.SCOTT LANEY: Now we're seeing almost all of these miners with mixed-dust pneumoconiosis, which includes silica and coal dust.HICKS: The National Mining Association represents coal companies, and they say safety measures to mitigate dusty mines have improved, and sick miners could have been exposed years ago, before new technology was in place. But Laney says there is no question in his mind, but the prevalence of black lung disease is still growing. In the research, he wrote, the data is a bellwether, not the remnant of an ongoing problem.LANEY: Nobody is doubting this whatsoever - I mean, especially if you live here in Appalachia like we do. You see it at the post office and the grocery store every day.HICKS: To curb this growing problem, the Federal Mine Safety and Health Administration created stricter limits on the amount of silica dust coal miners can legally be exposed to. But mining companies sued. The Mining Association says they support lower dust limits, but they want allowances for other methods to protect miners, like dust-filtering helmets. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has frozen enforcement indefinitely. That delay really frustrates Drew Harris, a lung doctor in southwest Virginia, who treats patients suffering with black lung disease.DREW HARRIS: It's outrageous that these are the numbers we see in 2026. We know how to prevent it. There's no mystery here. We need better protections to be enforced.HICKS: The Mine Safety and Health Administration declined to comment until the research letter was public. But legal briefs show the federal mining agency is holding private meetings around changing the safety rules. So for now, it's still unclear what future silica dust protections may or may not be in store for coal miners.For NPR News, I'm Justin Hicks in Norton, Virginia.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Correction Aug. 6th, 2026 An earlier version of this story mistakenly implied Congress imposed strict limits on exposure to coal mine dust in 1977. In fact, those limits were imposed in 1969. It also incorrectly said the federal black lung trust fund owes $3 billion to the U.S. Treasury; it owes $6.5 billion. And an earlier caption misidentified the person scrutinizing an X-ray image as radiologist Brandon Crum in Coal Run Village, Ky. The person is a clinician at New Beginnings Pulmonary Rehab in Norton, Va.

blocks.html_en: In recent decades, the biggest coal seams in Appalachia were mined out. Mining companies turned to the thinner seams that remained, digging through mountains to reach and then mine them. That requires cutting lots of rock, and in Appalachia, that rock typically contains quartz, which is rich in silica. The result is clouds of both coal dust and highly toxic silica dust.

sentences.en: Silica particles cause lungs to fight back with fibrotic tissue that builds and builds, severely inhibiting the ability to breathe.

sentences.zh: “煤炭的厚度并不存在，”肯塔基州和弗吉尼亚州的前矿工兼矿长蒂姆·巴尔蒂斯 (Tim Balthis) 解释道。

sentences.zh: 巴尔蒂斯在新起点肺康复中心发表了讲话，这是呼吸治疗师弗里曼拥有和经营的四家黑肺诊所之一。

sentences.en: The clinics help miners ease symptoms of the incurable disease.

blocks.html_en: "It's like opening your front door and letting the sunshine [in]" with dust particles floating in the light. "And then multiply that by 10 billion times. … It's like a fog," Balthis recalled.

sentences.en: Last year, the compliance rate hit 97%.

blocks.html_en: NIOSH first recommended tougher limits on silica dust exposure in coal mines in 1974. But for 50 years, both Democratic and Republican administrations failed to act. That finally changed in 2024, when the Biden administration succeeded in establishing a new silica dust regulation for mining. It made the exposure limit twice as restrictive. It also provided, for the first time, a direct regulatory response to overexposure, including imposition of even tougher exposure restrictions, and possible fines, for noncompliance.

sentences.zh: 但50年来，民主党和共和党政府都没有采取行动。

sentences.zh: 但采矿业提起诉讼，同意更严格的暴露限制，但不同意执行机制。

content_html_zh:
请随时关注我们每个工作日早上发送的 Up First 时事通讯。

呼吸治疗师马西·弗里曼不需要一项研究就能证实她回到了煤矿开采的黑暗时代。 她在 150 多个葬礼项目中找到了证据，这些项目都是为她位于弗吉尼亚州诺顿的肺康复诊所的前病人提供的。

“每一个都代表着一个因黑肺而消失的生命，”弗里曼一边翻阅着这些节目，一边认出名字和图像，解释道。

相关报道：NPR

“这些是丈夫。 他们是兄弟。 …… 这些人都是勤劳的人，他们唯一做的就是去工作养家糊口。 这让他们付出了一切。 …… 这就是黑肺的后果。”

根据周三发表在《美国呼吸与重症监护医学杂志》上的新数据，这种后果甚至比黑肺病临床医生和研究人员预期的还要可怕。

这些数据出现在联邦研究机构国家职业安全与健康研究所 (NIOSH) 的同行评审研究信中。

公共健康观察、肯塔基州公共广播电台和 NPR 在发表之前获得了 NIOSH 研究信的草稿。

NIOSH 研究人员发现，阿巴拉契亚中部的资深地下煤矿工人患上无法治愈且致命的肺部疾病的比例是近 50 年来最高的。

在肯塔基州、弗吉尼亚州和西弗吉尼亚州工作的矿工，在地下工作了至少 25 年的矿工患尘肺病或黑肺病的比例最高。 在过去五年中，三分之一（32.5%）的人在 NIOSH 进行的 X 射线检查中呈阳性。

上一次具有相同工作经历的矿工患病率如此之高是在 1978 年。 2018 年，NIOSH 上次报告该病发病率时，发病率为 20.6%。

新研究表明，即使在地下工作时间只有 15 年的矿工，黑肺病的发病率也更高，这是近 40 年来从未见过的。

相关报道：NPR

“我很反感，”NIOSH 研究流行病学家斯科特·莱尼 (Scott Laney) 说，他是这封研究信的主要作者。

“由于所有疾病已经在酝酿之中，情况不会好转。 这些人被视为一次性小部件，而不是人类。 …… 我们眼睁睁地看着他们死在我们眼前。”

根据 NIOSH 早期的一项研究，从 2020 年到 2023 年，超过 1,700 名煤矿工人死于黑肺病。

肯塔基州公共广播电台及其报道合作伙伴向联邦矿山安全与健康管理局 (MSHA) 提供了 NIOSH 调查结果的摘要，但该机构在看到已发布的报告之前拒绝发表评论或回答问题。

“煤矿工人的处境也好不到哪儿去”

新的发现“应该让任何对……怀有同情心的人感到震惊和震惊” 勤劳的人们，”前联邦矿山安全监管者、工作场所安全学者和倡导者塞莱斯特·蒙福顿 (Celeste Monforton) 说道。

“这是他们工作的结果，也是我们想要廉价电力的结果，”蒙福顿补充道。 “我们又回到了[近 50 年前]的状态。…… 煤矿工人的境况并不比[当时]好。”

相关报道：NPR

新发表的调查结果不包括用于确定疾病发生率的五年内接受测试或诊断的矿工人数。 但在回答《公共健康观察》和肯塔基州公共广播电台的问题时，NIOSH 表示，过去 5 年，它对阿巴拉契亚中部 280 名资深地下矿工进行了筛查，其中 91 人黑肺检测呈阳性。 该机构使用该样本来估计该地区所有类似矿工的费率，这是自 1974 年以来一直使用的方法。

新墨西哥大学医学院专门研究职业性肺病（包括黑肺）的临床和研究肺病学家阿克谢·苏德（Akshay Sood）说，NIOSH 研究人员在此应用的“整个过程”在我看来是有效的。 应 NPR、肯塔基州公共广播电台和公共卫生观察的要求，苏德审阅了 NIOSH 研究信函的草稿。

苏德总结说，美国国家职业安全卫生研究所的研究“强化了先前的观察结果，即尽管有现代粉尘控制法规，疾病患病率仍在继续增加”。

NIOSH 研究人员还写道，“多个外部指标...... 展示了与他们的发现一致的模式，包括过去十年中黑肺诊所诊断出的数千个新病例。

新估计的阿巴拉契亚中部地下矿工的患病率自 1999 年达到低点（仅为 7%）以来增加了四倍多。 30 年前，国会严格限制接触导致黑肺的煤矿粉尘。

从那时起，急剧下降的情况发生了逆转，特别是在阿巴拉契亚地区，根据对矿工进行测试和治疗的诊所收集的数据，那里有数千名矿工患有早期、晚期和致命阶段的疾病。 与专注于在职矿工的 NIOSH 不同，这些诊所往往会看到退休和下岗的矿工，他们在寻求肺部检查的同时试图获得州或联邦的黑肺福利。

煤矿关闭后，诊所里挤满了矿工。 美国劳工统计局的就业数据显示，过去十年，全美有超过 15,000 名煤矿工人失去了工作。

“这太可怕了，”肯塔基州煤润村的放射科医生布兰登·克拉姆说，他专门研究 X 光中的黑肺迹象。 2016 年，克拉姆首次记录到，在越来越年轻的煤矿工人中，严重黑肺病的发病率惊人地激增，而且病情迅速恶化。 NIOSH 研究人员和 NPR 调查证实了他的发现。

NIOSH 的新研究向 Crum 表明这种趋势仍在继续。

“这只是另一件事，证明了我们过去 10 年一直在说的话，”他说。 “这可能比我们想象的还要糟糕。”

领先的行业贸易团体国家矿业协会 (NMA) 也获得了 NIOSH 调查结果的摘要。 NMA 指出，NIOSH 在过去五年中报告的矿工患病率以及诊所诊断出的新病例并非源于目前煤矿中的硅尘暴露，因为疾病的形成和诊断可能需要数年时间。

NMA 发言人阿什利·伯克 (Ashley Burke) 在一份电子邮件声明中写道：“这意味着这些研究中讨论的事件涵盖了最初接触该病毒的矿工，他们的初次接触可以追溯到几年前，在许多情况下，可以追溯到几十年前。” “这些事件并不反映当今的条件、做法、保护或法规。”

尽管如此，矿工权益倡导者仍然担心，由于煤炭开采的重大变化导致危险的粉尘暴露，疾病高发率将持续下去。

切割岩石

近几十年来，阿巴拉契亚最大的煤层被开采殆尽。 矿业公司转向剩下的较薄的煤层，挖掘山脉，然后开采它们。 这需要切割大量岩石，而在阿巴拉契亚，这些岩石通常含有富含二氧化硅的石英。 其结果是形成煤尘和剧毒硅尘云。

新的 NIOSH 研究信称：“过量吸入煤矿粉尘是煤矿工人患上黑肺的唯一原因。” “大量证据表明，接触煤矿粉尘中的可吸入结晶二氧化硅成分在当代疾病模式中发挥着重要作用。”

NIOSH 流行病学家莱尼表示，根据暴露数据和放射线数据，硅尘和黑肺病之间存在很强的联系，这些数据显示出“暗示硅暴露”的异常现象。 他说，研究人员检查了尸检和移植后取出的肺部，“我们可以看到这些肺部中的二氧化硅。”

硅尘的毒性比单独的煤尘高 20 倍，并且含有容易吸入的细颗粒。 二氧化硅颗粒会导致肺部不断形成纤维化组织，严重抑制呼吸能力。

过去 25 年来在地下工作的煤矿工人目睹了导致更多硅尘暴露的变化。

“煤炭的厚度并不存在，”肯塔基州和弗吉尼亚州的前矿工兼矿长蒂姆·巴尔蒂斯 (Tim Balthis) 解释道。 他说，现在已经不像“爷爷”们开采大煤层的日子了。 “所以你必须采取更多的岩石，这反过来又会产生硅尘。”

巴尔蒂斯在新起点肺康复中心发表了讲话，这是呼吸治疗师弗里曼拥有和经营的四家黑肺诊所之一。 这些诊所帮助矿工缓解这种不治之症的症状。

57 岁的巴尔蒂斯患有所谓的复杂性黑肺病，即晚期且致命的阶段。 他试图向非矿工描述在地下煤矿的硅尘周围工作的感觉。

“这就像打开你的前门，让阳光进来”，灰尘颗粒漂浮在光线中。 “然后将其乘以 100 亿倍…… 就像雾一样，”巴尔蒂斯回忆道。

“成千上万的疾病机会”

美国国家矿业协会引用的政府数据显示，在过去 10 年里，硅尘暴露限值的遵守情况不断提高，全国范围内的采矿公司 90% 以上的时间都满足了这些限值。 去年，达标率达97%。

但高合规率并不意味着矿工受到充分保护。 一小部分过度暴露已导致数千起矿工面临风险。

肯塔基州公共广播电台和公共卫生观察分析了 MSHA 硅尘采样数据，发现自 2014 年以来，煤矿工人接触过量硅尘的次数超过 5,000 次。 二氧化硅颗粒的毒性非常大，很容易被吸入，而且很容易嵌入肺部，“数千次接触就相当于有数千次患病机会”，前监管者蒙福顿说。

事实上，2018 年 NPR 和 FRONTLINE 的一项调查在回顾 30 年的联邦数据时记录了 21,000 起过度接触硅尘的情况。 新闻机构还记录了越来越多患有复杂性黑肺病的退休和下岗矿工，自 2010 年以来这一数字已超过 4,000 人。

“与黑岩的恋情”

NIOSH 于 1974 年首次建议对煤矿中的二氧化硅粉尘暴露进行更严格的限制。 但50年来，民主党和共和党政府都没有采取行动。 这种情况终于在 2024 年发生了变化，当时拜登政府成功制定了新的采矿业硅尘法规。 它使暴露限制加倍严格。 它还首次对过度暴露做出了直接的监管反应，包括对违规行为实施更严格的暴露限制，并可能处以罚款。

但采矿业提起诉讼，同意更严格的暴露限制，但不同意执行机制。

联邦法院对行业诉讼做出了回应，诉讼还提到了其他问题，无限期推迟执行更严格的二氧化硅暴露限制。 特朗普政府并不反对推迟，并宣布推迟执行也将暂停。

相关报道：NPR

特朗普政府正在努力促进煤炭开采。 6月初，特朗普宣布拨款近7亿美元的联邦支出，用于维持燃煤发电厂和支持煤炭出口。

“煤炭是一项伟大的生意，”特朗普当时说道。 “论力量，没有什么比得上的了。”

蒙福顿说，政府似乎“对黑岩有一种情结，而不是对煤矿工人的情结、同情或关心”。

采矿公司需要通过地下强有力的通风来控制粉尘暴露。 采矿机还必须配备喷水装置来抑制灰尘。 但有时，它们的工作效果不够好，无法减少灰尘。

煤炭开采行业希望能够要求使用防尘口罩，以便在其他控制措施失败时矿工仍然可以工作。

NMA 的伯克说：“当其他控制措施不能充分降低暴露水平时，这些广泛的控制措施将辅以呼吸器，这与任何其他需要使用口罩以确保空气质量安全的职业没有什么不同。”

但联邦法律对待地下煤炭开采的态度与其他行业不同。 《矿山安全与健康法》要求煤矿公司防止“不安全和不健康的条件”，并确保矿工能够在“充分无可吸入粉尘”的工作条件下工作，这样他们就不会成为黑肺病的受害者。

防尘口罩和呼吸器也存在问题。 许多接受 NPR 采访的矿工抱怨说，口罩会在危险和嘈杂的环境中影响沟通，被灰尘堵塞，​​工作温度太高，并且无法滤除更细的颗粒。 针对防尘口罩公司的诉讼已导致数百万美元的判决和和解。

即使是更现代的设备也存在问题，包括将新鲜空气推过脸部并位于透明防护罩后面的头盔。 MSHA 在其 2024 年二氧化硅粉尘法规中指出，头盔“不是永久解决方案”，因为它们使有效沟通变得困难，并且可能限制周边视力和态势感知，从而使工作变得危险。

弗吉尼亚大学肺病学家、弗吉尼亚州石山黑肺诊所的医疗主任德鲁·哈里斯博士直接谈到了对煤矿工人的延迟保护。

“我们需要采取行动，我们需要采取行动的意愿，”哈里斯断言。 “我们需要加强我们知道将有助于消除这种疾病的保护措施。”

“那些没有发言权的人”

哈里斯位于弗吉尼亚州西南部的石山健康服务中心的黑肺诊所比全国任何一家诊所接待的矿工都多，诊断出的疾病病例也多。 阿巴拉契亚各地煤炭县的矿工纷纷涌向石山，因为这里提供检测、治疗和黑肺福利索赔的法律帮助。

哈里斯称 NIOSH 的新发现“令人震惊”。 但根据他在诊所看到的情况，这些结果并不令人惊讶。 仅在过去 5 年里，Stone Mountain 就诊断出了 2,400 例新的黑肺病例。

哈里斯说：“如果你想象三分之一的学校教师因为在工作中接触到某种东西而患上无法治愈的肺部疾病，那么整个国家都会举手尖叫，并立即停止这种接触。” “[但是]这在很大程度上影响了阿巴拉契亚农村居民，他们没有发言权，没有国家团结在他们身后。”

疾病发病率的不断上升导致矿工源源不断地寻求州和联邦的生活和医疗费用福利。 根据劳工部向国会提交的一份报告，2024 年，超过 26,000 名矿工或其幸存家属从联邦黑肺信托基金提取了 1.75 亿美元。

据 NMA 称，矿业公司向该基金捐款超过 230 亿美元，但破产和保险不足将部分负担转嫁给了纳税人。 该基金欠美国财政部超过 65 亿美元。

根据 NIOSH 的一项研究，公共资金支付了越来越多的肺移植费用，每项费用高达 200 万美元，而且主要是为阿巴拉契亚中部的矿工提供的。

对于像蒂姆·巴尔蒂斯这样的矿工来说，黑肺负担让生活本身充满挑战。 由于肺部纤维化组织堆积，即使是最简单的任务也很困难。 呼吸变得越来越费力。 他知道情况只会变得更糟。 除非他有资格进行肺移植，否则他很可能会因此而死亡。 但即便如此，对于煤矿工人来说，中位生存率也不足七年。

“这就像你的男子气概上的伤口。” 巴尔蒂斯说，他指出，他携带并使用“紧急吸入器”，以便与孙子们有超过几分钟的玩耍时间，甚至在教堂唱歌。

“几位医生都说我应该已经死了...... 我告诉他们……“上帝还没有结束我的生活。” 我一直顺服他，现在他要把我交还给我的孙子们……他对我还没有结束。”
